messages.author: 8c44de84988a8def
messages.subject: density covariates
parts:
I am analyzing line transect data collected in seven regions of a
large study area. The main goal of the project is to investigate
which factors affect density of different species. Possible factors
are hunting pressure, distance to road and vegetation. Unfortunately,
for most species encounter rates are fairly low so that I need to use
a global detection function. From what I read in this list and in the
literature this makes a statistical comparison of densities quite
complicated (need for bootstrapping etc.). Royle et. al (2004)
proposed a model that allows covariates for abundance/density and
this was recently implemented in the R package "unmarked". I run a
test dataset with that package and results with covariates on density
are fairly similar to results from Distance with stratification. The
big advantage I see is that I should be able to use a model selection
approach based on AIC to see which model best fits the data.

My main question is if this approach is valid for my question and if
there are any pitfalls I should be aware of.

Thanks,

Mathias

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: density covariates
parts:
I've not used the software but in principal it is fine. Only pitfall is
the assumed Poisson distribution. Using covariates for density means
that it is fitting an inhomogeneous Poisson process (IPP) and that can
absorb some variation in density but it is likely that there is still
over-dispersion which means that std errors for density and abundance
may be underestimated. I haven't widely broadcast it, but there is a
pacakge called DSpat on CRAN that fits IPPs for distance sampling but it
does so using point data. It works for nice sampling regimes with
rectangular non-overlapping transects but it needs some more coding to
be useful for most practical situations. It works with grids whereas I
believe unmarked would work at a transect level. That would be most
useful for point transects where the entire circle is probably in the
same habitat. Lines are more likely to sample a gradient of features. I
believe the Royle article used point data. That's my 2 cents. --jeff
